expect: A student investigates the specific heat capacity of water. She heats 0.50 kg of water using a 50 W immersion heater for 4.0 minutes and records a temperature rise of 11°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity from her results and suggest one reason why it differs from the accepted value of 4200 J/kg°C.
value: A student investigates the specific heat capacity of water. She heats 0.50 kg of water using a 50 W immersion heater for 4.0 minutes and records a temperature rise of 5.0°C. Calculate the specific heat capacity from her results and suggest one reason why it differs from the accepted value of 4200 J/kg°C.
note: F2: 12 000 J into 0.50 kg of water can raise it by at most 5.7 degC, so a rise of 11 degC is impossible and it made the calculated value come out at half the accepted one. Heat loss always makes a measured specific heat capacity too HIGH, so the stated reason contradicted the arithmetic. A rise of 5.0 degC gives 4800 J/kg degC, which heat loss does explain.

expect: Energy supplied: \(E = P \times t = 50 \times 240 = 12\,000\) J (1). \(c = E \div (m \times \Delta T) = 12\,000 \div (0.50 \times 11) = 12\,000 \div 5.5 \approx 2180\) J/kg°C (1). Calculated value is lower than accepted value (1). Reason: heat is lost to the surroundings / the container / the air, so not all energy goes into the water (1). Evaluation of experimental design — e.g. adding insulation or a lid would reduce heat loss (1).
value: Energy supplied: \(E = P \times t = 50 \times 240 = 12\,000\) J (1). \(c = E \div (m \times \Delta T) = 12\,000 \div (0.50 \times 5.0) = 12\,000 \div 2.5 = 4800\) J/kg°C (1). Calculated value is higher than the accepted value (1). Reason: heat is lost to the surroundings / the container / the air, so not all the energy supplied went into the water (1). Evaluation of experimental design — e.g. adding insulation or a lid would reduce heat loss (1).
note: F2: recomputed for the corrected temperature rise, and the direction of the error now matches heat loss.
